$comment: England & Wales, International Criminal Law - immunity ratione materiae does not shield conduct that is itself a crime under international law/jus cogens, and its legislative successor in the ICC Act 2001's domestic core-crimes regime. Pinochet No 3 [1999] UKHL 17 predates BAILII/Find Case Law live access in this environment; verified via the citing-judgment method through Jones v Kingdom of Saudi Arabia [2004] EWCA Civ 1394, which quotes Pinochet's own speeches verbatim with pinpoint paragraph references. Note that Pinochet No 3 does not itself cite or apply the ICC Act 2001 (it predates the Act by two years and concerns torture under the UN Torture Convention/Criminal Justice Act 1988 s.134) - this entry pairs them as sequential steps on the same doctrinal line (case establishes the immunity principle; statute codifies the jurisdictional model for the ICC's own core crimes), not as a direct construes/applies relationship, and the edge below is labelled accordingly.
verification_method: International Criminal Court Act 2001 s.51(1)-(2) fetched live and directly from legislation.gov.uk, independently re-fetched and word-for-word consistent on both attempts. R v Bow Street Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate, ex parte Pinochet Ugarte (No 3) [1999] UKHL 17 verified via the citing-judgment method: Jones v Kingdom of Saudi Arabia [2004] EWCA Civ 1394 fetched live and directly from Find Case Law, independently re-fetched with paragraph 54's quotation of Lord Browne-Wilkinson confirmed in substance.

authorities.name: International Criminal Court Act 2001, s.51
authorities.date_note: Enactment year. The text verified this session is the current in-force version.
authorities.proposition: It is an offence against the law of England and Wales for a person to commit genocide, a crime against humanity, or a war crime (s.51(1)) - the domestic-effect provision that makes the Rome Statute's three core crimes prosecutable as ordinary English/Welsh criminal offences. The offence applies to acts committed in England or Wales, or committed abroad by a UK national, UK resident, or person subject to UK service jurisdiction (s.51(2)) - extraterritorial reach notwithstanding any official position the accused may hold.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session, on two independent passes, word-for-word consistent both times.

authorities.name: R v Bow Street Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate, ex parte Pinochet Ugarte (No 3)
authorities.judge_or_panel: Lord Browne-Wilkinson, Lord Goff, Lord Hope, Lord Hutton, Lord Saville, Lord Millett, Lord Phillips of Worth Matravers
authorities.proposition: A former head of state has no immunity ratione materiae in English proceedings for conduct that is itself a crime under international law and has acquired jus cogens status - official capacity cannot convert such conduct into a protected 'state function.' On the facts, if Pinochet organised or authorised torture after the relevant date, he was not acting in a capacity that gives rise to immunity ratione materiae, because such actions were contrary to international law.

Corroborated for date, panel, and outcome via two independent secondary sources (Oxford Public International Law's case report and Wikipedia). Recorded at VERIFIED_SECONDARY_SOURCE given the citing-judgment paraphrase rather than a fully verbatim primary quote.

edges.verified_via: Pinochet No 3 [1999] UKHL 17, per its quotation in Jones v Saudi Arabia [2004] EWCA Civ 1394 para 54: establishes that immunity ratione materiae does not shield international crimes, a principle Parliament separately codified two years later for the ICC's own core crimes in s.51 - a sequential doctrinal link, not a direct construes/applies relationship, since Pinochet No 3 does not itself cite the ICC Act 2001.

what_this_is_not: Two nodes on the same doctrinal line (immunity does not shield international crimes) rather than a direct statute-construing-case pairing - the relationship is sequential, not interpretive, and is labelled accordingly. Does not cover universal jurisdiction procedure under the ICC Act 2001's arrest-warrant provisions, the Rome Statute's complementarity principle, or any other International Criminal Law subject - all remain unbuilt.
